To drat something means to mildly curse it — to direct a small, harmless expression of frustration or annoyance at something. Think of it as the verbal equivalent of lightly shaking your fist at something that has annoyed you.

It is a softer, gentler substitute for the word damn used as a verb. When someone says "drat it," they are essentially saying "damn it," but in a way that is far milder, more old-fashioned, and completely inoffensive.

"Drat" in its verb form is a transitive verb, which means it must act on something — it needs an object. You don't just "drat" into thin air. You drat something specific that has caused your frustration.

The most classic and common construction is:

"Drat + it / this / that / [the thing that annoyed you]!"

• "Drat it!" — The most common usage. The speaker is directing a mild verbal curse at the situation or thing that just went wrong.
  • "Drat this rain!" — The speaker is frustrated by the rain and is cursing it in a gentle way.
  • "Drat the luck!" — Cursing one's bad fortune.
  • "Drat that cat — it knocked over my cup again!" — Mildly cursing the cat for causing a small annoyance.

In every case, the speaker is not literally casting a spell or wishing serious harm. It is purely an emotional release — a way of verbally venting at something.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

This is important to understand, because the feeling of a word is part of knowing it fully.

"Drat" carries a very specific emotional temperature: it is mild, quaint, and almost charming. It signals frustration, yes — but frustration that is small, momentary, and harmless. It does not carry the weight or sharpness of stronger swear words.

Because of this, it tends to appear in a few specific contexts:

  • Old-fashioned or period-style writing and speech — characters in older novels, plays, or films might say "Drat!" where a modern character might use something stronger.
  • Whimsical or humorous contexts — someone using "drat" today is often doing so with a light, self-aware, or slightly theatrical flair.
  • Family-friendly settings — because it is so mild, it has long been used as a safe substitute for stronger language, especially around children.

• It does not mean to physically strike or harm something.
  • It is not a serious or powerful curse. Nobody fears being "dratted."
  • It is not commonly used in formal writing or serious professional contexts.

If you want to lock this word in your memory, hold onto this one idea:

To drat something = to aim a tiny, toothless curse at it out of mild frustration.

It is the verbal equivalent of a sigh, an eye-roll, or a gentle groan — just shaped into a single, slightly dramatic word. It says: "This thing has annoyed me, and I want the world to know it," but in the most harmless, even lovable, way possible.
